note: National organizations are real; local listings are illustrative samples.

respite_grants.name: ARCH National Respite Network and Resource Center
respite_grants.what_they_offer: A national respite locator that helps caregivers find respite providers and programs in their state, plus guides on choosing and paying for respite.
respite_grants.eligibility: Open to any family caregiver looking for respite options.
respite_grants.how_to_apply: Use the respite locator on the ARCH website to search by state and type of care, then contact listed programs directly.

respite_grants.name: State Lifespan Respite Programs
respite_grants.what_they_offer: Many states run Lifespan Respite programs that coordinate respite resources across ages and disabilities, and some offer short-term respite vouchers or caregiver-directed respite funds.
respite_grants.eligibility: Varies by state; many programs serve family caregivers of children and adults with disabilities or special needs.
respite_grants.how_to_apply: Search for your state's Lifespan Respite program through ARCH, or ask your state's aging and disability resource center.

respite_grants.name: Medicaid home and community-based waiver respite
respite_grants.what_they_offer: Many state Medicaid home and community-based services waivers include respite hours as a covered service for eligible children and young adults with disabilities.
respite_grants.eligibility: Varies by state and waiver; some waivers look only at the child's needs and income, and many have waiting lists.
respite_grants.how_to_apply: Contact your state Medicaid agency or developmental disabilities agency and ask which waivers include respite and how to join the waiting list.

respite_grants.name: Easterseals local affiliates
respite_grants.what_they_offer: Easterseals affiliates across the country offer disability services, and many provide respite, day programs, or camps for children and young adults with disabilities.
respite_grants.eligibility: Varies by affiliate and program.
respite_grants.how_to_apply: Find your nearest affiliate on the Easterseals website and ask about respite or camp programs.

respite_grants.name: The Arc chapters
respite_grants.what_they_offer: Local chapters of The Arc support people with intellectual and developmental disabilities and their families; some chapters offer respite, family support, or help navigating waiver services.
respite_grants.eligibility: Varies by chapter; focuses on intellectual and developmental disabilities.
respite_grants.how_to_apply: Find your local chapter on The Arc's website and ask about family support and respite.

respite_grants.name: National Family Caregiver Support Program (through Area Agencies on Aging)
respite_grants.what_they_offer: Federally funded caregiver support delivered locally, which can include respite, counseling, training, and information. It specifically includes older relatives, such as grandparents, raising children.
respite_grants.eligibility: Includes grandparents and other relatives age 55 and older caring for a child, among other caregiver groups; details vary by local agency.
respite_grants.how_to_apply: Find your local Area Agency on Aging through the Eldercare Locator and ask about family caregiver support and respite.

respite_grants.name: Parent Training and Information Centers
respite_grants.what_they_offer: Every state has at least one federally funded Parent Training and Information Center that helps families of children with disabilities understand their rights and find local resources, including respite programs.
respite_grants.eligibility: Families and caregivers of children and youth with disabilities, birth through 26.
respite_grants.how_to_apply: Find your state's center through the Center for Parent Information and Resources and call or email for help.

respite_grants.name: Golden Hour Respite Fund (sample listing)
respite_grants.what_they_offer: Sample listing: small grants to pay a trained respite provider for a few hours each month so caregivers can rest, run errands, or simply sit in the sun.
respite_grants.eligibility: Sample listing: caregivers of children 0 to 21 with physical disabilities living in the metro Atlanta area.
respite_grants.how_to_apply: Sample listing: short online form plus a letter from any provider who knows the child.

respite_grants.name: GrandFamily Breather Grants (sample listing)
respite_grants.what_they_offer: Sample listing: respite and weekend-break funding for grandparents and relatives raising children with disabilities.
respite_grants.eligibility: Sample listing: kinship caregivers in Maricopa County raising a child with a physical disability.
respite_grants.how_to_apply: Sample listing: apply by phone with help from a kinship navigator.

respite_grants.name: Resource Family Rest Network (sample listing)
respite_grants.what_they_offer: Sample listing: a pool of trained, accessible-home respite providers for foster and resource families caring for children who use mobility equipment.
respite_grants.eligibility: Sample listing: licensed foster and resource families and approved kinship caregivers.
respite_grants.how_to_apply: Sample listing: request a referral through your placement worker.

respite_grants.name: Saturday Sunrise Accessible Play Club (sample listing)
respite_grants.what_they_offer: Sample listing: a free monthly Saturday morning of adaptive play, art, and music for kids, with trained volunteers, while caregivers take three hours off.
respite_grants.eligibility: Sample listing: children ages 3 to 14 using wheelchairs, walkers, or canes, and their siblings.
respite_grants.how_to_apply: Sample listing: register online two weeks in advance.

respite_grants.name: Brazos Break Respite Vouchers (sample listing)
respite_grants.what_they_offer: Sample listing: caregiver-directed vouchers you can use to pay a trusted relative, neighbor, or provider for respite care.
respite_grants.eligibility: Sample listing: caregivers in Central Texas of children with disabilities who are on a waiver waiting list.
respite_grants.how_to_apply: Sample listing: one-page application and proof of residence.

respite_grants.name: Harbor Nights Overnight Respite (sample listing)
respite_grants.what_they_offer: Sample listing: fully accessible overnight respite weekends with nurses on site, including ceiling lifts and roll-in showers.
respite_grants.eligibility: Sample listing: young people ages 6 to 21 with complex physical disabilities in the Baltimore region.
respite_grants.how_to_apply: Sample listing: intake call and a care-planning visit.

respite_grants.name: Next Chapter Young Adult Hangouts (sample listing)
respite_grants.what_they_offer: Sample listing: evening social outings for young adults 16 to 21 with physical disabilities, with accessible transportation, giving caregivers a regular night off.
respite_grants.eligibility: Sample listing: young adults in the Seattle area and the families who support them.
respite_grants.how_to_apply: Sample listing: sign up for the monthly calendar by text.

respite_grants.name: Regional Center of the East Bay: respite services
respite_grants.what_they_offer: Eligible East Bay families can ask their regional center service coordinator about funded respite hours.
respite_grants.eligibility: Children and adults found eligible for regional center services (Alameda & Contra Costa counties).
respite_grants.how_to_apply: Ask your RCEB service coordinator to add respite to your Individual Program Plan.

respite_grants.name: Caregiver to Caregiver (C2C) Respite Network (Federation for Children with Special Needs)
respite_grants.what_they_offer: Matches Massachusetts families of children who need specialized support so caregivers can trade respite, based on the child's medical and support needs, location, and language or cultural preferences. Staff run background checks, offer trainings and online forums, and check in with matched families at least monthly.
respite_grants.eligibility: Massachusetts families of children and young people ages 0-26 who need specialized support; open to families regardless of financial resources.
respite_grants.how_to_apply: Click Join / Request a Match on the C2C page or email c2crespite@fcsn.org.

respite_grants.name: Massachusetts DDS Family Support Centers: respite and flexible family support
respite_grants.what_they_offer: Department of Developmental Services-funded centers give families information, referrals, and support services; eligible families can ask about respite, including flexible funds to pay respite providers they choose.
respite_grants.eligibility: Information and referral are open to any family; funded respite generally requires eligibility for DDS services (intellectual and developmental disabilities).
respite_grants.how_to_apply: Contact the Family Support Center for your area from the DDS directory, or ask your DDS Service Coordinator about respite.

respite_grants.name: True Friends weekend and weekday respite
respite_grants.what_they_offer: DHS-licensed short-term respite at Camp Eden Wood in Eden Prairie and Camp Friendship in Annandale, with weekend, weekday, and Saturday options, so caregivers can rest while kids enjoy camp.
respite_grants.eligibility: Children and adults ages five and up with developmental or physical disabilities.
respite_grants.how_to_apply: Complete True Friends' online program application and health questionnaires; ask which funding sources (such as waiver funds) they can accept.

respite_grants.name: Minnesota Family Support Grant (can help pay for respite)
respite_grants.what_they_offer: A state cash grant for families raising a child with a certified disability at home; respite care is one of the listed uses.
respite_grants.eligibility: Children under 25 with a certified disability living in their family home, under an income limit; generally not available alongside disability waivers, PCA/CFSS, or the Consumer Support Grant. Funding is limited and there may be a waiting list.
respite_grants.how_to_apply: Apply through your county or tribal human services office (in Hennepin County, start with disability services) or ask the Disability Linkage Line.

respite_grants.name: Lifespan Respite Washington voucher (run by PAVE)
respite_grants.what_they_offer: A voucher of up to $1,000 per household per year for short-term respite from a provider on the approved list; it usually lasts about 3-4 months, and summer camp and recreation awards start in January. Family members, friends, and independent providers can't be paid with the voucher.
respite_grants.eligibility: Unpaid Washington caregivers who provide 40 or more hours of care per week (including supervision), can't afford respite on their own, and aren't enrolled in another respite program (unless waitlisted and not scheduled within 30 days). The person receiving care can be any age.
respite_grants.how_to_apply: Submit the online application; for help email getrespite@wapave.org or call 253-442-3214. Awards depend on available funding.

respite_grants.name: DSHS Developmental Disabilities Administration (DDA): respite for children and youth
respite_grants.what_they_offer: DDA serves eligible children and youth ages 0-21 with developmental disabilities so they can live at home. Ask whether respite can be part of your child's services; DDA also runs Enhanced Respite Services, short-term stays in DDA-contracted, licensed, staffed settings for some children and youth.
respite_grants.eligibility: Children and youth found eligible as DDA clients; DDA decides whether a child's condition meets its developmental disability definition.
respite_grants.how_to_apply: Use DDA's How to Enroll page or Service and Information Request Form; current clients can ask their Case Resource Manager about respite.

support_groups.name: Parent to Parent USA
support_groups.schedule: One-to-one matches arranged on request through local and statewide programs.
support_groups.description: A national network of Parent to Parent programs that match caregivers of children with disabilities or special health care needs with a trained volunteer who has walked a similar road.

support_groups.name: Generations United GrandFamilies
support_groups.schedule: Ongoing resources and network events; see website.
support_groups.description: Generations United's grandfamilies work supports grandparents and other relatives raising children, with resources, policy updates, and connections to kinship support in your area.

support_groups.name: Sibling Support Project and Sibshops
support_groups.schedule: Sibshops are hosted locally on their own schedules; online groups run ongoing.
support_groups.description: Lively, playful workshops and online communities for brothers and sisters of kids with disabilities, so siblings get peer support and a whole lot of fun.

support_groups.name: Little Lobbyists
support_groups.schedule: Ongoing online community and advocacy actions.
support_groups.description: A family-led group advocating for children with complex medical needs and disabilities, helping caregivers share their stories and connect with each other.

support_groups.name: Washington State Fathers Network
support_groups.schedule: Groups meet on varying schedules across Washington; contact the network for current times.
support_groups.description: A long-running network supporting fathers and father figures of children with special health care needs and developmental disabilities.

support_groups.name: Grand Circle Coffee Hour (sample listing)
support_groups.schedule: Sample listing: first and third Tuesday, 10:00 to 11:30 a.m.
support_groups.description: Sample listing: grandparents raising grandkids who use wheelchairs and walkers swap tips on IEPs, lifts, and keeping up with teenagers, over very good coffee.

support_groups.name: Resource Family Roundtable (sample listing)
support_groups.schedule: Sample listing: second Thursday, 6:30 p.m., with childcare provided.
support_groups.description: Sample listing: foster and resource families caring for children with physical disabilities share wins, navigate school transfers, and learn the rights of foster parents at the IEP table.

support_groups.name: Rooted and Rising: BIPOC Caregiver Circle (sample listing)
support_groups.schedule: Sample listing: every other Sunday, 7:00 p.m. Eastern.
support_groups.description: Sample listing: a space for Black, Indigenous, Latine, Asian American, and other caregivers of color to talk about raising disabled children while navigating bias in schools and medical settings, with lots of joy in the room.

support_groups.name: The Pit Crew: Dads, Granddads, and Uncles (sample listing)
support_groups.schedule: Sample listing: Wednesdays, 8:30 p.m. Eastern, after bedtime.
support_groups.description: Sample listing: fathers, grandfathers, uncles, and other men raising kids with physical disabilities talk wheelchair repairs, adaptive sports, and the feelings no one asks them about.

support_groups.name: Familias en Movimiento (sample listing)
support_groups.schedule: Sample listing: Saturdays, 10:00 a.m., in Spanish.
support_groups.description: Sample listing: a Spanish-language group for caregivers of children with disabilities, covering IEP rights, Medicaid, and community, with snacks and music.

support_groups.name: Rainbow Rollers Family Circle (sample listing)
support_groups.schedule: Sample listing: last Friday of each month, 7:00 p.m. Pacific.
support_groups.description: Sample listing: LGBTQ+ caregivers, including two-mom and two-dad families, raising children with disabilities, sharing everything from school forms that fit your family to Pride parade wheelchair routes.

support_groups.name: Kin Together (sample listing)
support_groups.schedule: Sample listing: Mondays, 6:00 p.m.
support_groups.description: Sample listing: aunts, uncles, cousins, and older siblings who stepped up to raise a relative's child with a disability, talking guardianship, school enrollment, and holding family together.

support_groups.name: Next Steps: Transition Caregivers Group (sample listing)
support_groups.schedule: Sample listing: first Monday, 7:30 p.m. Eastern.
support_groups.description: Sample listing: caregivers of teens and young adults 14 to 21 explore transition IEPs, supported decision-making, ABLE accounts, and cheering on first jobs.

support_groups.name: Sunday Sibs Hangout (sample listing)
support_groups.schedule: Sample listing: second Sunday, 2:00 p.m.
support_groups.description: Sample listing: games and real talk for brothers and sisters ages 8 to 16, while caregivers connect in the next room.

support_groups.name: Joy Circle Open Gathering (sample listing)
support_groups.schedule: Sample listing: Thursdays, 7:00 p.m., in person with a video link.
support_groups.description: Sample listing: an open-door group for every kind of caregiver, starting each session with a win of the week.

support_groups.name: Sweet Tea Grandfamilies (sample listing)
support_groups.schedule: Sample listing: fourth Saturday, 11:00 a.m., at a community center.
support_groups.description: Sample listing: Black grandparents and great-grandparents raising grandchildren with disabilities share wisdom, faith, and practical help with schools and benefits.

support_groups.name: DREDF Parent Training & Information Center (free IEP help)
support_groups.schedule: Call or email for advocate support and workshops
support_groups.description: Free help for East Bay families of children and young adults with disabilities (birth to 26): understanding IEPs, preparing for meetings, and support for foster families and foster youth.

support_groups.name: CPAC: Connecticut Parent Advocacy Center (free IEP help)
support_groups.schedule: Call or email for one-on-one help and workshops
support_groups.description: Connecticut's statewide Parent Training and Information Center: free support for families of children with any disability, from birth to 26, including help preparing for IEP meetings.

support_groups.name: Federation for Children with Special Needs: Parent Training & Information Center (free IEP help)
support_groups.schedule: Information Center staffed 10 a.m.-3 p.m., Monday-Friday; free workshops across Massachusetts
support_groups.description: Massachusetts' Parent Training and Information Center, and the nation's first, offers free help to families, youth, and young adults with questions about special education: understanding IEPs, IEP clinics, workshops, and help in many languages.

support_groups.name: Family TIES of Massachusetts & Parent to Parent of Massachusetts
support_groups.schedule: Call or email to be matched with a support parent and to join trainings
support_groups.description: Staffed by family members with lived experience, Family TIES helps families of children birth to 26 with special health needs, disabilities, or medical complexity find resources, and Parent to Parent matches you with a trained support parent who has walked a similar path.

support_groups.name: Boston Special Education Parent Advisory Council (SpEdPAC)
support_groups.schedule: Monthly general meetings and trainings during the school year; check the SpEdPAC website for dates
support_groups.description: The independent, districtwide council of Boston Public Schools families of students with IEPs, run by parent volunteers who give families a voice and support. All families are welcome.

support_groups.name: PACER Center: Minnesota's Parent Training & Information Center (free IEP help)
support_groups.schedule: Contact an advocate by phone or email; free virtual and in-person workshops
support_groups.description: Minnesota's federally designated Parent Training and Information Center and Family-to-Family Health Information Center. Advocates (in English, Spanish, Somali, and other languages on request) help families of children and young adults with disabilities understand options and prepare for IEP meetings.

support_groups.name: Family Voices of Minnesota: CONNECTED parent-to-parent support
support_groups.schedule: Virtual peer-led parent support groups; call or email to request a one-on-one parent match
support_groups.description: A family-run nonprofit where parents and caregivers raising children with disabilities or special healthcare needs support each other: virtual support groups, a Parent Support Navigator, and matches with a trained parent whose child has similar needs.

support_groups.name: PAVE Parent Training and Information Center (free IEP and 504 help)
support_groups.schedule: Contact PAVE for one-on-one help; live trainings are offered in person or online
support_groups.description: Washington's Parent Training and Information Center gives free one-on-one help and trainings to family caregivers and youth with disabilities (birth to 26), including help organizing concerns before IEP and Section 504 meetings. PAVE also runs Lifespan Respite Washington and the Family to Family Health Information Center.

support_groups.name: The Arc of King County Parent to Parent
support_groups.schedule: Online support groups on Facebook and Google Groups, plus community events; email to request a Helping Parent match
support_groups.description: Peer support from parents who've walked the road before: support groups, community events, and Helping Parent matches that connect you with a trained mentor parent with similar experiences. Services are offered in English and Spanish.

resets.title: Box breathing in the car line
resets.best_for: Waiting in the school pickup line before a hard conversation or a big after-school transition.
steps: Put the car in park and rest both hands on the wheel.
Breathe in through your nose for a count of four.
Hold gently for four.
Breathe out slowly for four, then hold for four.
Repeat the box for about five minutes, letting your shoulders drop a little each round.

resets.title: 5-4-3-2-1 in the waiting room
resets.best_for: Therapy, specialist, or IEP meeting waiting rooms when your mind is racing ahead.
steps: Name five things you can see, including one that is a color you love.
Name four things you can feel, like your feet on the floor.
Name three things you can hear.
Name two things you can smell, or two scents you love.
Name one thing you are proud of your child for this week.

resets.title: Rolling walk meditation
resets.best_for: A stroll with your child in a wheelchair or stroller, or walking beside them as they roll or use a walker.
steps: Pick a short, easy route and agree to go slow.
Match your breath to the rhythm of wheels or steps.
Notice three things in the sky, then three things at ground level.
Point out one beautiful thing to each other.
End with a high five or a fist bump.

resets.title: Joy jar note
resets.best_for: The end of a long day, especially one that felt like all paperwork.
steps: Grab a scrap of paper and a pen.
Write one moment today that made you laugh or smile.
Add one thing your child did that delighted you.
Fold it and drop it in a jar on the counter.
On rough days, pull out three notes and read them out loud.

resets.title: Shoulder release stretch
resets.best_for: After lifting, transfers, or carrying equipment, when your shoulders are up by your ears.
steps: Sit or stand tall with your feet planted.
Roll your shoulders back slowly five times, then forward five times.
Drop your right ear toward your right shoulder and breathe for three breaths; switch sides.
Clasp your hands behind your back and gently open your chest.
Shake out your hands like you just finished a great dance.

resets.title: Voice memo vent
resets.best_for: Right after a frustrating phone call with insurance, a school, or a vendor.
steps: Open your phone's voice memo app.
Set a timer for three minutes and say everything you are feeling, no filter.
Take one big breath when the timer goes off.
Record one more sentence: what is one next step you can take?
Delete the vent or save it; the point was to let it out.

resets.title: One-song kitchen dance party
resets.best_for: Late afternoon slumps or when everyone in the house needs a mood shift.
steps: Pick one song that makes you feel unstoppable.
Turn it up loud enough to mean it.
Move however your body wants: sway, wave, roll, bob your head.
Invite your child to choose a dance move everyone copies.
Finish with a big group cheer.

resets.title: Hand on heart, kind words
resets.best_for: Moments of guilt or worry, especially at night after the house goes quiet.
steps: Sit somewhere comfortable and place one hand on your heart.
Take three slow breaths and feel your hand rise and fall.
Say quietly: 'I am doing a hard thing, and I am doing it with love.'
Name one thing you handled well today, even if it was small.
Let yourself rest for one more minute before you get up.
